answer:
I built GHZ states of 2, 3, 4, and 5 qubits. In a GHZ state, all the qubits are linked so that a measurement gives either all 0s or all 1s, with even odds. I put the 4 circuits into one job with 100 shots each. I ran that job on the free test device sirius:mock first (job 01a16058-5e25-75ab-b2bb-2bf8fa1bd7d6). That run only checked that the job was built correctly, because the mock device returns placeholder results that do not depend on the circuit. Then I ran the same job once on the real Sirius QPU (job 01a16058-aa1a-718b-b2b6-e27ed3096bc9). The API reported 1.0 billed second for it, which is about 0.30 credits.

On a perfect machine, 100% of shots would show all bits agreeing. On the real machine, the share of shots where all bits agreed was 94% for 2 qubits, 92% for 3 qubits, 80% for 4 qubits, and 80% for 5 qubits. The shots that did agree were split roughly evenly between all 0s and all 1s, which is what a GHZ state should give. For example, the 5-qubit circuit gave 47 shots of 00000 and 33 shots of 11111.

The trend shows that noise grows as the state gets bigger. Each extra qubit adds one more two-qubit gate. On Sirius it also adds two more MOVE operations through the central resonator, plus one more qubit that can be misread. Every operation has a small chance of error, and one error anywhere is enough to break the agreement. So the error chances add up, and the agreement fraction falls as size grows. The 4-qubit and 5-qubit results are equal here. With only 100 shots, each fraction has an uncertainty of about 4 to 5 percentage points, so that flat step is within statistical noise and the overall downward trend still holds. One limit applies: agreement only tests the all-0 and all-1 pattern. A full check of entanglement would also need measurements in other bases, and this job did not include those.
